I'm Eshaan, Chinmay's older brother, and I've seen this before. At the dosa place on Sunday the menu had forty kinds of dosa. Chinmay read every line out loud: masala, onion, paneer, cheese, mysore... The waiter came twice. Papa said, "Just pick, beta."
Finally he said "cheese" very fast, like jumping into cold water. When the plates came, he kept looking at my mysore masala. He ate half of his, then said, "I should've got that one."
Last month at the chaat stall, with only four things on the board, he picked in a second and was happy. I'm not sure what goes on in his head, but long menus seem to make him miserable.

qa.q: How many kinds of dosa were on the menu?
qa.a: The menu had forty kinds of dosa.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay have felt unsure even after ordering?
qa.a: With forty options, each seemed possibly better than the one he picked, so seeing his brother's mysore masala made his own dosa feel like a mistake.

qa.q: What could Papa try next time at the dosa place?
qa.a: He could ask Chinmay to choose from three dosas he likes, so the choice is quick and Chinmay can enjoy his plate.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see his brother's menu troubles?
qa.a: Eshaan has seen it before and compares it with the happy chaat stall visit, but admits he can't be sure what Chinmay is thinking.

grounding: An older brother describes a boy who takes ages over a long menu and then wishes he had ordered something else.

Friday: At the new ice-cream parlour there were thirty-two flavours. Lokesh walked up and down the glass for ten minutes while his friend Baljeet finished a whole cone. He chose blueberry, took two licks, and said, "Chocolate chip looks better." He didn't finish it.
Next Friday: Same shop. Lokesh started reading every label again. Baljeet said, "Only look at the first row. Pick from those." Lokesh grumbled but chose mango.
Two weeks later: Lokesh walked in, looked only at the first row, said "Butterscotch", and ate every bit, humming.

qa.a: There were thirty-two flavours.

qa.a: He was thinking he had chosen wrong, that chocolate chip looked better, so the blueberry lost its taste for him.

qa.q: Which tip turned things around for Lokesh, and why did it work?
qa.a: Baljeet's rule to look only at the first row, because fewer flavours made the choice quick and left Lokesh happy with it. 😊

qa.q: What was it like for Baljeet to wait while Lokesh chose on the first Friday?
qa.a: Baljeet finished a whole cone while Lokesh walked up and down, so the wait was probably long and a bit boring.

grounding: Shows over weeks how a boy dithers and regrets his pick from many flavours, then enjoys choosing from a short row.

passage:
Jatin, you took twenty minutes with that menu today, and then sulked about your pizza. Let your Ramesh Dadu tell you something.
When I was nine, my uncle took me to a big sweet shop in the old city. "Choose any one sweet," he said. There were rows and rows: jalebi, rasgulla, barfi, sohan halwa, fifty kinds. I walked up and down so long the shopkeeper started laughing.
At last I pointed at the pink barfi. The moment I bit it, I saw my cousin's hot jalebi and thought, why didn't I pick that? I don't even remember the taste of the barfi, only the jalebi I didn't have.
In our village shop there were four sweets, and I was always happy.

qa.q: Which sweet did young Ramesh pick in the end?
qa.a: He pointed at the pink barfi.

qa.q: Why did the barfi lose its charm for young Ramesh as soon as he bit it?
qa.a: After weighing fifty kinds, he felt unsure, so seeing his cousin's hot jalebi made him feel he had picked wrong.

qa.q: What could Jatin try the next time a menu is long?
qa.a: Jatin could pick three things that sound good and choose among only those, like the four-sweet village shop.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel hearing Dadu's story?
qa.a: Jatin may feel less embarrassed about sulking, knowing Dadu felt the same as a boy, and may laugh at the barfi and jalebi.

grounding: A grandfather recalls being a boy who agonised over a huge sweet counter and then wished he had picked something else.

passage: The bus would leave the highway dhaba in fifteen minutes, and the conductor had already honked once. Harish held the menu, four pages long: parathas with nine fillings, three kinds of chole, noodles, lassi in five flavours. His older sister Parul had ordered in ten seconds. "Just pick, Harish." He read the paratha list again. Aloo? Gobi? Paneer? Mooli? The waiter tapped his pencil. When the horn went a second time, Harish blurted, "Aloo paratha!" It came hot and fast. He took two bites, then stared at the man at the next table eating paneer paratha. "Mine's boring," he muttered. "I should have got that one." Back on the bus, he was still talking about paneer.

qa.q: How long was the menu at the dhaba?
qa.a: The menu was four pages long.

qa.q: Why did Harish feel his aloo paratha was boring after only two bites?
qa.a: With so many other fillings on the menu, the paneer paratha at the next table looked like the better choice he'd missed, so his own felt uncertain and less tasty.

qa.q: What could Harish try the next time he meets a long menu?
qa.a: He could decide on two things he likes before reading every page and pick one quickly, so there are fewer options left to wonder about.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt while the conductor honked?
qa.a: She was probably anxious about missing the bus and impatient with her brother, even if she could see he was stuck.

grounding: Under time pressure, a boy takes ages over a long menu, finally picks and then wishes he had chosen something else.

passage: Pema's mother had promised both children one drink each at the juice bar in their Mumbai market after swimming class. Pema chose mango in a second. Varun stood under a board of forty juices and shakes: kiwi-mint, chikoo, watermelon-basil, cold coffee, pineapple-ginger... He read from top to bottom, then back up again. Pema had finished half her glass. "Chikoo," he said at last. Then, "No, wait, watermelon-basil." The juice-wala sighed and made it. Varun sipped, frowned and looked at Pema's orange glass. "Yours looks nicer," he said. "Maybe I should've picked mango. Or the kiwi one." He drank slowly, still reading the board.

qa.a: There were forty juices and shakes.

qa.q: How did Varun feel about his juice, and what shows it?
qa.a: Varun felt unsure and a bit disappointed with his choice, frowning at his watermelon-basil, saying Pema's looked nicer and still reading the board.

qa.q: What small step would help Varun choose faster and enjoy his drink more next time?
qa.a: He could choose from just two or three he already likes instead of reading all forty, so there are fewer what-ifs afterwards.

qa.q: What might Pema's mother be thinking as Varun read the board up and down?
qa.a: She might be amused but also a bit impatient, and puzzled that a simple treat turned into so much worry for him.

grounding: A boy faced with a huge drinks board takes ages, then doubts his pick because the other options seem better.

passage: When our school canteen got a new menu last term, I was so excited. I'm Vishal, and before, there were only four things: samosa, vada pav, idli and poha. Now there were twenty-five: sandwiches, noodles, three kinds of dosa, frankies, milkshakes. On the first day I stood in front of the board so long that the bell rang and I had to grab a cheese sandwich. I didn't even like it. The next day I got noodles and kept looking at Francis's masala dosa. Every day I wondered if I'd picked wrong. Francis just ate dosa every single day and looked happy. After two weeks I decided to copy Francis. Now it's dosa on Monday and a frankie on Thursday. I stopped reading the board.

qa.a: Vishal felt unsure and unsatisfied, because with so many choices every meal seemed less certain and someone else's plate always looked better.

qa.a: Vishal fixed a simple plan, dosa on Monday and a frankie on Thursday, and stopped reading the board, which ended the daily comparing.

passage:
Parent's note after Dhruv's birthday dinner, Sunday. Mahima.
We took Dhruv to the new family restaurant for his ninth birthday. The menu was eight pages long, with pictures. He spent twenty minutes turning pages back and forth, asking what everything tasted like, while the waiter came and went three times. Finally he chose the pasta. When it came, he looked at the next table's pizza and his face fell. "I should have got pizza." Then it was the burger he wanted. He barely ate. On the drive home I realised I had done the same to him with birthday presents: 'Choose anything!' Next time I'll give him two or three options, and let the rest go.

qa.q: How many pages long was the menu?
qa.a: The menu was eight pages long.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv's face fall when he saw the next table's pizza?
qa.a: Dhruv felt disappointed and unsure, because after so many options his pasta seemed less right than whatever he hadn't picked.

qa.q: What does Mahima plan to do next time, and why?
qa.a: Offer Dhruv two or three options, because fewer choices make it easier to pick and to enjoy what he picked.

qa.q: What might the waiter have thought, coming back three times?
qa.a: The waiter might have felt a little impatient, but probably understood a child lost in a long picture menu.

grounding: Shows a child taking ages over a long menu and then wishing he had picked something else, noticed by a parent.

Jagdish, you've been staring at that ice cream menu for ten minutes. Let me tell you about my brother Manu at the Baisakhi mela, when he was nine and I was twelve.
Our Bapuji gave him one coin and said, "One thing. Anything." There were sixty stalls: balloons, whistles, a snake charmer, toy guns, sugar candy, a giant wheel. Manu ran from stall to stall all afternoon, touching everything, choosing nothing. He was sure the next stall would have something better.
At the end, the stalls were closing. In a hurry he bought the nearest thing, a paper windmill. On the bullock cart home he cried, because he'd wanted the tin whistle.
The next year Bapuji said, "Choose from three stalls only." Manu got the whistle and blew it for a month.
I, Ritu, still have that whistle.

qa.q: What did Manu buy in a hurry?
qa.a: Manu bought a paper windmill.

qa.q: Why did Manu cry on the bullock cart?
qa.a: Manu felt disappointed and regretful, having rushed to buy a windmill when he had really wanted the tin whistle.

qa.q: Which moment in the story helped Manu, and why?
qa.a: Bapuji's rule the next year, choose from three stalls only, made the choice easy and satisfying.

qa.q: How might Bapuji have felt watching Manu run from stall to stall?
qa.a: Bapuji was probably amused and a little worried, seeing Manu too caught up to choose.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a boy at a fair who could not choose among sixty stalls and regretted his hurried pick.
